name: Grand Duchy of Moscow & Tsardom of Russia
summary: A small principality around Moscow that grew, under Mongol overlordship and then on its own, into the Tsardom of Russia. By 1700 it reached the Pacific; in 1721 Peter the Great renamed it the Russian Empire.

knownFor.label: Moscow Kremlin
knownFor.note: The fortress whose red-brick walls and cathedrals were rebuilt by Italian architects under Ivan III.

knownFor.label: Saint Basil’s Cathedral
knownFor.note: Built on Red Square to celebrate the conquest of Kazan.

knownFor.label: Streltsy
knownFor.note: Musket-armed infantry set up by Ivan IV, the first standing army of Russia.

location.value: Began around Moscow on the upper Volga; by 1700 stretched from the White Sea and Ukraine’s left bank to the Pacific.
location.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

terrain.value: Dense forest to the east and a large network of rivers, such as the Volga and Oka, that helped trade.
terrain.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow (checked 8 Nov 2026)

climate.value: Long, cold winters and a short growing season.
climate.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

resources.value: Furs were the main export; fish and salt were traded inside the country.
resources.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow (checked 8 Nov 2026)

disasters.value: The Black Death reached Russia in 1352–1353 and killed perhaps a quarter of the population.
disasters.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow (checked 8 Nov 2026)

population.value: About 6 million around 1500; about 13–15 million by 1700.
population.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

urbanisation.value: Mostly rural; Moscow was one of the largest cities in Europe (perhaps 100,000–200,000 by 1600).
urbanisation.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

disease.value: The Black Death (1352–1353), which killed Grand Prince Simeon and Metropolitan Theognostus.
disease.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow (checked 8 Nov 2026)

migration.value: Peasants fled south and east to escape serfdom, becoming Cossacks; settlers moved into Siberia.
migration.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

economicBase.value: Farming by peasants, most of whom stayed free until the 16th century, and river trade.
economicBase.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow (checked 8 Nov 2026)

tradeRoutes.value: The Volga route to Persia; White Sea trade with England from 1553, and later with Holland, through Arkhangelsk (founded 1584).
tradeRoutes.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

wealth.value: Collecting tribute for the Mongol khan from other Russian princes made Moscow rich.
wealth.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow (checked 8 Nov 2026)

moneyAndTax.value: The ruble; taxes collected per household; the Copper Riot (1662) followed debasing the coinage.
moneyAndTax.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

inequality.value: Serfdom was fully legalised in the 1649 law code (Sobornoye Ulozheniye).
inequality.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

governmentType.value: A monarchy of grand princes; Ivan IV was crowned the first Russian tsar in 1547.
governmentType.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow (checked 8 Nov 2026)

keyRulers.value: Ivan I Kalita. Dmitry Donskoy. Ivan III (1462–1505). Vasily III. Ivan IV (1533–1584).
keyRulers.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow (checked 8 Nov 2026)

succession.value: Father to son; the end of the Rurik line in 1598 led to the Time of Troubles until the Romanovs were elected in 1613.
succession.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

institutions.value: The Boyar Duma (council of nobles), the Zemsky Sobor (assembly of the land), government departments (prikazy).
institutions.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

stability.value: The Oprichnina terror under Ivan IV (1565–72); the Time of Troubles (1598–1613); revolts of Stenka Razin (1670–71).
stability.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

eliteConflict.value: Powerful boyar clans, such as the Belskys, Glinskys and Shuyskys, competed for influence while Ivan IV was a child.
eliteConflict.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow (checked 8 Nov 2026)

armyAndTech.value: Cavalry levies of nobles; streltsy musketeers; regiments trained in the Western way (“new order”) from the 1630s.
armyAndTech.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

majorWars.value: Defeated Mamai's Tatar army at the Battle of Kulikovo (1380); long wars with Lithuania ended in 1503.
majorWars.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow (checked 8 Nov 2026)

territoryChange.value: Annexed Novgorod (1478) and took Tver (1485); under Ivan III the state tripled in size.
territoryChange.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow (checked 8 Nov 2026)

alliancesRivals.value: Under Golden Horde rule until Ivan III defeated the Tatars in 1480; its great rival was the Grand Duchy of Lithuania.
alliancesRivals.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow (checked 8 Nov 2026)

inventions.value: Cannon casting (the Tsar Cannon, 1586); the first printed books in Moscow (Ivan Fyodorov, 1564).
inventions.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

scienceEducation.value: Learning mostly in monasteries; the Slavic-Greek-Latin Academy opened in 1687.
scienceEducation.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

openness.value: Cautious towards foreigners, who lived in a separate “German quarter” in Moscow; Peter I opened the country to Western ideas.
openness.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

communicationTransport.value: Rivers carried trade; people paid for a postal relay service called the yam.
communicationTransport.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow (checked 8 Nov 2026)

religion.value: Russian Orthodox Christianity; Moscow became its spiritual centre, and Russian bishops chose their own metropolitan in 1448.
religion.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow (checked 8 Nov 2026)

languageWriting.value: Church Slavonic was the literary language; government offices wrote in a form closer to everyday speech.
languageWriting.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow (checked 8 Nov 2026)

artsArchitecture.value: The Moscow school of icon painting led by Andrei Rublev; stone churches in the Kremlin, such as the Dormition Cathedral (1475–1479).
artsArchitecture.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow (checked 8 Nov 2026)

socialStructure.value: Grand prince, boyars, a service class of nobles, clergy, merchants and a vast majority of peasants.
socialStructure.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow (checked 8 Nov 2026)

sharedIdentity.value: The Orthodox faith and the idea of a shared "Russian land".
sharedIdentity.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow (checked 8 Nov 2026)

dailyLife.value: Wooden log houses (izba) with a big stove; rye bread, cabbage soup (shchi), kasha and kvass.

neighbours.value: The Golden Horde, the Khanate of Kazan, the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, Novgorod and Tver.
neighbours.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow (checked 8 Nov 2026)

ideasReligions.value: Orthodox Christianity; after Constantinople fell in 1453, Moscow adopted the idea of an Orthodox tsardom.
ideasReligions.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow (checked 8 Nov 2026)

colonisation.value: Ivan III campaigned east against the principalities of Yugra, whose princes swore allegiance in 1483.
colonisation.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow (checked 8 Nov 2026)

riseSignals.value: Ivan I collected tribute for the Mongol khan from other Russian princes, which increased Moscow's wealth.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow (checked 8 Nov 2026)

peakPeriod.value: Under Ivan III the state tripled in size; in 1547 Ivan IV was crowned tsar.
peakPeriod.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow (checked 8 Nov 2026)

declineSignals.value: The Time of Troubles nearly destroyed the state, with Polish troops in Moscow (1610–12).
declineSignals.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

outcome.value: Became the Russian Empire under Peter the Great in 1721.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

sources.value: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia; Riasanovsky, A History of Russia.
sources.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia

overallCertainty.value: Political events are well documented; population figures are estimates.
overallCertainty.source: Wikipedia: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Wikipedia: Tsardom of Russia
